newsitem.title: FRANCE: Brokers divided on Paris bourse short-term outlook.
newsitem.headline: Brokers divided on Paris bourse short-term outlook.

text.p: The Paris Stock Exchange is headed higher this year but the bourse's near-term outlook divided the brokers, stock analysts and fund managers interviewed by Reuters on Monday.

Some operators said the bourse was due for a correction after a rapid rise that lifted the CAC 40 index to all time highs on Monday morning, but others said technical indicators suggested it may climb further before hitting resistance.
"The market should head toward 2,410 points, and then 2,480 within the next three to five weeks," said Pierre Vignaud, a technical analyst at brokerage EIFB.

"The fundamentals are good for the bourse, and they haven't changed -- interest rates are low, corporate profits are expected to improve on moderate economic growth, productivity is improving, and exchange rates are favourable with the franc's decline against the Italian lira, British sterling and dollar," said George de Nesmeskery Kiss, economist at Societe Generale.
Brokers said further restructuring measures anticipated in the drugs, financial and retail sectors were also positive for the bourse.
"The market has accelerated a lot, and there is a risk of a short-term correction," said Daniel Dourmat at Caisse Centrale des Banques Populaires.
Dourmat said he expected the CAC, trading at 2,360.08 at 1530 GMT, to rise in the first half of the year to up to 2,450 points but level off in the second half ahead of legislative elections.

Portfolio manager Valery Monin at Sogeposte said she expected the market to rise early in the year on expectations of stronger corporate earnings. But she said she expected profit-taking to follow the results.
"The market is rising very fast, with increasing volatility, and that's making us feel cautious," she told Reuters.
While most eyes were on the events on Wall Street, some brokers, including Dourmat, were unnerved by the weakness of the Tokyo market.
Dourmat was concerned its fragility could spread if Japanese investors were obliged to sell assets abroad to cover losses at home.
Pierre Amancic, deputy director of IFF Bourse, said the bourse had risen so fast that it risked an abrupt correction.
"The indicators are signalling that the market is overbought. There's a risk of a violent retracement that could take us back as far as 2,200 points," he said.
He said he was also concerned that the recent buying appeared to be driven by professional traders rather than investment funds.
